S01.text: Coffee prices are falling! Great! Maybe spring will finally come to my wallet, too. But supermarket prices do not change. They look calm, as if saying, News? I haven't heard any. If bean prices have fallen, why don't we pay less? First, let's go back to when high prices caused a stir. Bad weather in Brazil and Vietnam hurt the supply. Few beans were for sale, and stocks were low. Then demand around the world was strong. It was a hard mix for prices to settle down. At about the same time, ICE's future prices for arabica coffee reached a record high. But future prices are not prices for green beans sold right away. They are not store prices, either. They may all wear the same name tag, coffee price, but they mean different things.

S02.text: US roasters keep green beans in stock. Then they roast and pack them. Reports also say price talks with stores often happen every 3 months. There are several steps between the beans and the store shelf. Even when market prices fall, not every step responds, Got it, cut prices now! Of course, around 9 months is an estimate from market experts and others. It is not a timer for every company. It is not a promise that prices will definitely be lower 9 months from now. It is too soon to circle a sale on your calendar. In other words, a fall in market prices is not an update button for price tags. The prices on shelves may reflect purchases and talks from some time ago. Next time you see a headline about falling prices, ask the price tag. Say, By the way, how many months ago did you get here?

S03.text: After that, an index showing world market prices fell by 25% over 7 months. The USDA links this drop to extra supplies becoming easier to get. But in the United States, the coffee part of the Consumer Price Index was still higher than in the same month a year earlier. Wait a minute, that doesn't add up! You might want to say that. But one is a world market index, and the other is the US Consumer Price Index. One shows a drop over 7 months, while the other compares prices with a year earlier. They are on different stages and run on different clocks. If you pour the numbers into the same cup, the story gets muddled. And price tags follow their own schedule. Market experts and others interviewed by Reuters estimated that it takes around 9 months or longer for green-bean prices to show up in store prices. If market prices are a breaking news alert, price tags are patient letters.

S04.text: About 24 hours and 48 minutes later, at 11:04 a.m. on July 14, Trump made another post. He said the 20% plan would be replaced by trade and investment projects between Gulf states and the US. He cited very productive discussions with Middle Eastern leaders. He also said no one should charge ships in the Strait. He said he disliked fees. The change was sudden. But the dates must stay separate to understand the oil move. On July 13, Brent rose 9.59% and settled at $83.30. Reuters linked that rise to concern about a US sea blockade of Iran. The blockade was planned for the next day. Reuters also linked it to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

S05.text: This news feels like a short play in 3 acts. The first act was 20%. Act 2 brought an unexpected turn. Act 3 was an unexpected move in oil prices. The curtain rose on July 13. At 10:16 a.m., Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe. But 20% was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay, how the money would be collected, or what legal basis would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage. The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

S09.text:
ELLE included mini bags among its fall and winter 2026 style trends. Its examples included Khaite’s palm-sized evening clutch and Chanel’s novelty minaudière. They mostly hold the basics: a phone, wallet, keys, and lip products. They cannot compete with roomy bags for storage. Their job is visual. They add a special feeling. They say, “This is today’s mood.”

We see the season more clearly by looking at bags beside them.

S10.text: Vogue also covered the 2026 season. It showed small pouches from Prada and Loewe. It also showed Celine's Ultra Maxi and Altuzarra's large shoulder bag. It showed roomy totes from Toteme and other brands, too. This list matters. Large bags had not disappeared. Small and large bags appeared in the same season. We are not seeing mini bags spread through the whole market. Instead, they are back in fashion reports and on certain runways. Even so, trends now look different. Bags no longer play a game with only one size on the throne. Large bags are the luggage crew. They carry what we need. Mini bags are the stage crew. They catch the eye and set the mood. In 2026, the runway proudly shows this split in their work.

S12.text: This episode examines a test of an AI service that makes phone calls for users. It shows how people working behind an AI service can raise concerns about privacy and trust. Listen to learn why this matters when AI is used to handle everyday tasks.

S13.text: Some people may speak or feel differently if they think they are talking to AI. Knowing they are talking to a person may change that. Even if the request goes well, we cannot ignore the missing notice. We cannot just say, It all worked out in the end. That was exactly what Meta admitted it had got wrong. Convenience matters. But some people care just as much about knowing who they are talking to. If AI passes the baton to a person, it should say so. That one line is part of the service, too. The person taking over does not have to be a secret guest.
